name: Spiral of silence
statement: People who sense their view is losing ground say less about it, so the opinion that looks dominant grows louder and its rival drops out of public view.
meaning: The theory joins two claims of different sizes. The small one is about a person: someone who reads the climate of opinion as hostile to their own view becomes less willing to voice it. Her 1974 paper puts two things inside that fear, the fear of separation and doubt about one's own capacity for judgement, so the cause is not fear alone. The large one is about a society: because everyone is reading everyone else, small differences in who speaks compound over time, and one side is established as public opinion while the other falls silent. Noelle-Neumann's definition follows from the second claim. Public opinion is the opinion that can be voiced without fear of sanction. Nearly all the empirical work tests the first claim, at one moment, with a survey question, and the gap between what is claimed and what is measured is the subject of most of the argument about the theory.

origin.note: Her article is a condensed version of a longer German paper in a Festschrift for Arnold Gehlen, which carried 33 tables of survey results. The English-language book, The Spiral of Silence: Public Opinion, Our Social Skin, followed from the University of Chicago Press in 1984, translated from Die Schweigespirale.

evidence: Noelle-Neumann drew on Allensbach institute surveys run mostly in 1971 and 1972, each with 1,000 to 2,000 structured interviews on representative cross-sections of the population. Twelve controversial topics were put to respondents between January 1971 and November 1972, from abortion law to keeping Willy Brandt as Chancellor. Willingness to speak was measured by asking people to imagine a conversation among passengers on a long train journey and to say whether they would enter it. Her first table pools 9,966 interviews and reports that 36% would discuss the topic, 51% would not and 13% were undecided. That table's footnote names four topics only: socialism, a ban on the Communist Party, Chancellor Brandt and unmarried couples living together. It is not a figure for all twelve. The central table concerns socialism in August 1972. Among people who thought socialism would establish itself and welcomed it, 53% would join the train conversation; among those who thought the same and feared it, 28% would, on bases of 229 and 388. The pattern held separately among the politically interested and the uninterested. Two of the twelve topics ran the other way. On the treaties with Moscow and Warsaw, and on more influence for Franz Josef Strauss, minorities of 17 to 25% were at least as willing to speak as majorities of 53 to 61%. Noelle-Neumann read that as a hard core who will not conform, some of whom may have grown used to isolation.

replication.headline: The individual-level correlation turns up again and again and is tiny; the spiral itself is rarely tested, and where it has been it runs in opposite directions in different countries.
replication.detail: Matthes, Knoll and von Sikorski pooled 66 studies with more than 27,000 participants and report r = .10 between perceived opinion support and political opinion expression. They found the relationship no weaker online than offline, and no variation by the number or opinion of the people being addressed, by climate characteristics, or by design, measurement and sample features. The largest silencing effect, r = .34, came when people talked to family, friends or neighbours about obtrusive issues. Their reading is that the relationship is stronger and more robust than previously thought. Only the abstract their publisher deposited at Crossref could be read here, and it does not say what that comparison is with. The obvious candidate is the earlier meta-analysis by Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan, which could not be opened either. Xu, Liu, Kim and Chon give its figure as an average r = 0.054 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.028 to 0.080, and that number reaches this page through them rather than through the paper. Both meta-analyses cover the static micro test only. Thurre, Gale and Staerklé went at the macro claim instead, using eight rounds of the European Social Survey from 2002 to 2016 across 15 countries and 195,194 respondents, with signing a petition, wearing or displaying a campaign badge and joining a lawful demonstration as the dependent variable. Pro-immigration opinion was associated with speaking out in all 15 countries, but the direction of movement over 14 years split: pro-immigration voices lost ground in France, Ireland and Switzerland and gained it in Germany, Hungary, Poland and the UK. They tested a second issue, and it ran the other way. Pro-EU respondents were significantly less likely to speak out in Finland, Ireland, Poland, Switzerland, Sweden and the UK, and no more likely anywhere. Their conclusion is that a single time point cannot diagnose a spiral, and that a carefully timed static test would still have reached misleading conclusions in several of those countries.

study.cite: Matthes, J., Knoll, J., & von Sikorski, C. (2018). The "spiral of silence" revisited: A meta-analysis on the relationship between perceptions of opinion support and political opinion expression. Communication Research, 45(1), 3-33.

limits: The train question asks what a person imagines they would do. No validation of it against observed behaviour was found on 21 September 2026, in Crossref and OpenAlex searches or in the reference lists of the papers read here. Three studies come closer, and all three changed the answer. Hayes, Shanahan and Glynn gave people six topics to discuss with a real group, and their abstract reports a relationship much larger than the average in the 1997 meta-analysis, without saying how much larger. Hayes, Uldall and Glynn staged actual conversations with trained confederates who produced a climate either agreeing or disagreeing with the participant, and found the climate moved expression only among people who scored high on the Willingness to Self-Censor Scale. Scheufele, Shanahan and Lee put the hypothetical question against a real invitation to join a focus group, and found willingness lower and more strongly tied to fear of isolation. Only publisher abstracts of those three were read here. Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan's meta-analysis could not be obtained at all, so its pooled figure, its study count and its moderator tests are reported here at second hand or not at all. Thurre and colleagues flag social desirability as a rival explanation for their pro-immigration results, and note that their outspokenness measure is generic rather than tied to the specific issue.
misreadings: The famous version of the train test has a five-hour journey in it. The 1974 article describes only a conversation among passengers on a long train journey and puts no length on it. The theory is also cited as though it predicted uniform silencing, which its own first paper does not: two of the twelve topics produced a minority at least as willing to speak as the majority, and Noelle-Neumann said so. Pew Research Center's 2014 study is the most quoted modern evidence and is widely described as showing that social media silences people. It surveyed 1,801 American adults between 7 August and 16 September 2013 about the Snowden surveillance disclosures, and asked what they would be willing to say, not what they had said. Of those asked, 86% were willing to discuss the story in person and 42% of Facebook and Twitter users were willing to post about it; of the 14% unwilling to discuss it in person, 0.3% would post about it. That is a difference between two hypothetical willingness measures. The pooled correlation is the other trap. An r of .10 across 66 studies is a real relationship and a weak predictor of any individual's behaviour, and it is evidence for the conformity step rather than for the spiral the theory is named after.

sources.text: Noelle-Neumann, E. (1974). The spiral of silence: A theory of public opinion. Journal of Communication, 24(2), 43-51. Read in full, as a nine-page PDF of the published article found on an open course site, after Wiley and Oxford Academic both answered a Cloudflare bot challenge. Every figure on this page from the 1974 article was checked against that copy, whose title page carries the correct author, affiliation and pagination.

Noelle-Neumann, E. (1984). The spiral of silence: Public opinion, our social skin. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. Translated from Die Schweigespirale. Not read. The Internet Archive scan is lending-restricted and its text file is refused, so the publisher, year and subtitle here come from the Open Library record alone.

Matthes, J., Knoll, J., & von Sikorski, C. (2018). The "spiral of silence" revisited: A meta-analysis on the relationship between perceptions of opinion support and political opinion expression. Communication Research, 45(1), 3-33. Read only as the abstract Sage deposited at Crossref. Sage's own PDF answers a Cloudflare bot challenge, and no repository copy was found at Vienna or through Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar on 21 September 2026. Every figure quoted here appears in that abstract.

Glynn, C. J., Hayes, A. F., & Shanahan, J. (1997). Perceived support for one's opinions and willingness to speak out: A meta-analysis of survey studies on the "spiral of silence". Public Opinion Quarterly, 61(3), 452-463. Not obtained on 21 September 2026. Oxford Academic answers a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall notice, Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it as closed, and nothing was found in the Ohio State or Cornell repositories or on the authors' pages. Crossref and OpenAlex hold no abstract for it. Its pooled correlation is quoted on this page from Xu and colleagues rather than from the paper.

Xu, L., Liu, J., Kim, J., & Chon, M.-G. (2021). Are Chinese netizens willing to speak out? The spiral of silence in public reactions to controversial food safety issues on social media. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(24), 13114. Source for the 1997 meta-analysis figure quoted here. Read in full from the Europe PMC full-text XML after MDPI's own PDF answered an Akamai access denial. Its reference 39, which carries the figure, is the Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan meta-analysis.

Thurre, F. O., Gale, J., & Staerklé, C. (2019). Speaking up or silencing out in the face of rising right-wing populism: A dynamic test of the spiral of silence across 15 European countries. International Journal of Public Opinion Research, 32(3), 547-568. Published online in October 2019 and in print in 2020. Read in full as the authors' accepted manuscript in the Lausanne repository, not as the version of record, which is closed. The manuscript's text and the publisher's deposited abstract agree on the sample, the countries and the survey rounds.

Hayes, A. F., Shanahan, J., & Glynn, C. J. (2001). Willingness to express one's opinion in a realistic situation as a function of perceived support for that opinion. International Journal of Public Opinion Research, 13(1), 45-58. Read only as the abstract Oxford deposited at OpenAlex, after Oxford Academic answered a Cloudflare bot challenge. The abstract names the six topics and the real group, and says the correlation was much larger than the 1997 meta-analytic average without giving a number.

Hayes, A. F., Uldall, B. R., & Glynn, C. J. (2010). Validating the willingness to self-censor scale II: Inhibition of opinion expression in a conversational setting. Communication Methods and Measures, 4(3), 256-272. Read only as the abstract Taylor and Francis deposited at OpenAlex, after the publisher answered a Cloudflare bot challenge. The abstract carries the two confederates, the manipulated climate and the finding that only dispositional self-censors were moved.

Scheufele, D. A., Shanahan, J., & Lee, E. (2001). Real talk: Manipulating the dependent variable in spiral of silence research. Communication Research, 28(3), 304-324. Read only as the abstract Sage deposited at OpenAlex; the publisher answers a Cloudflare bot challenge.

Hampton, K., Rainie, L., Lu, W., Dwyer, M., Shin, I., & Purcell, K. (2014). Social media and the 'spiral of silence'. Pew Research Center, 26 August 2014. Read in full from the published report, which gives the sample, the field dates and all three percentages quoted here.
